sharedText: observe to perform every word of command
reason: Registered because the observation is worth keeping even though the verse cannot be pinned. 'They did obey and observe to perform every word of command with exactness' uses the King James Bible's standing formula for covenant obedience — 'observe to do' occurs in eighteen KJV verses, thirteen of them in Deuteronomy — and applies it to a captain's orders in the field rather than to the commandments of God. That transfer is the interesting thing and the register is the place for it; no single Deuteronomy verse can be the source of an eighteen-fold formula, and 'observe to perform' occurs in no KJV verse at all. Deuteronomy 5:32 is named here rather than any of the other seventeen for a reason a later pass should see: it is the one that continues 'ye shall not turn aside to the right hand or to the left', which is the formula this catalogue has just linked at Alma 56:37 to 2 Samuel 2:19. The two phrases are adjacent in Deuteronomy 5:32 and eleven chapters apart in Helaman's letter, which is a coincidence worth recording and not enough to move the 56:37 link, where the singleton 'turned not to the right hand' and the pursuit setting both point to 2 Samuel.

sharedText: there was not one soul of them which did perish
reason: A cross-reference, not a rejection. 'There was not one soul of them which did perish' is the second statement of the claim adjudicated at Alma 56:56, where 'there had not one soul of them fallen to the earth' reproduces the King James Bible's fixed formula for the preservation of a threatened young man ('there shall not one hair … fall to the earth', 1 Samuel 14:45, 2 Samuel 14:11, 1 Kings 1:52). Here the formula is dropped and only the claim survives — 'perish' for 'fall to the earth' — so this verse has the theology of 56:56 without its wording, and the wording is where the argument lives. Sent to 56:56. Note that 57:25 adds the qualification that makes the whole sequence coherent: not one perished, and not one was unwounded.

A cross-reference. 'Whosoever did not doubt, that they should be preserved by his marvellous power' is the third appearance in two chapters of the negated-doubt conditional adjudicated at Alma 56:47, against Matthew 21:21's 'if ye have faith, and doubt not' (a KJV singleton) and Mark 11:23's 'shall not doubt in his heart'. Helaman is quoting the mothers' teaching back at the moment it is vindicated, so this is the writer repeating his own report rather than the King James Bible a second time. Sent to 56:47. Worth noting for the variant register that the 1830 reading here is 'marvellous', the King James spelling, which later editions modernize — see CONVENTIONS §8; the phrase 'marvellous power' is in no KJV verse, so nothing hangs on it beyond the orthography.

sharedText: blessed is the name of our God
reason: 'And blessed is the name of our God: for behold, it is he that hath delivered us.' The doxology is real and it is adjudicated in this book at Alma 19:12, against Daniel 2:20's 'Blessed be the name of God for ever and ever' — one of only three KJV verses carrying 'blessed be the name'. The rest of Gid's sentence will not carry a row of its own. 'Delivered out of the hands of our enemies' is the Book of Mormon's own plural formula, used eight times from Mosiah 9:17 onward, and the KJV's four instances all read 'hand' (1 Samuel 4:3, 12:10, 2 Samuel 19:9, Luke 1:74); 'hath done this great thing for us' is close to 1 Samuel 12:24's singleton 'how great things he hath done for you' and to 1 Samuel 12:16's 'this great thing', but neither is close enough to displace the corpus formula, and the Book of Mormon's own Mark 5:19 borrowing for that idea was adjudicated long before, at 1 Nephi 7:11. Sent to 19:12.

The second occurrence in two chapters, and declined for the reasons given at Alma 56:52: 'took courage' occurs in exactly two KJV verses (2 Chronicles 15:8, Acts 28:15) but the Book of Mormon has made the phrase its own across a dozen passages from 1 Nephi 4:35, and both KJV instances are of a godly man heartened by God's word or God's people. Here it is Lamanite prisoners heartened by the cry of an approaching army, and the courage carries them onto Nephite swords in the next verse. Sent to 56:52.

sharedText: have entered into the rest of their God
reason: The closest call in this chapter. 'Entered into his rest' is a KJV singleton at Hebrews 4:10 and 'enter into his rest' is a second singleton at Hebrews 3:18, and Alma 57:36's perfect — 'the souls of them which has been slain, have entered into the rest of their God' — matches Hebrews 4:10's tense rather than 3:18's infinitive, which is a real distinction and an argument for a fresh row. Two things hold it back. Hebrews 3:18 is already adjudicated in this book at Alma 13:6, on the same four words and with the mediation against Psalm 95:11 settled there; and 'the rest of the Lord' is by this point the Book of Mormon's own standing phrase, running from Alma 12:36-37 and 13:12-16 through 16:17 to 60:13 and Moroni 7:3, so the possessive here is the corpus formula rather than a second reach for Hebrews. Recorded at length because the possessive form does have its own KJV singleton — Hebrews 4:9's 'a rest to the people of God' — which Alma 13:6 does not account for, and a later pass may reasonably decide this row differently. Sent to 13:6.
